notes: Custody time limit extension quashed for failure to enquire at other London courts.

enrichment.short_title: Armstrong: custody time limit extension remitted for multi-court listing enquiry
key_facts: Leonard Armstrong challenged HH Judge Bing's extension of custody time limits from 17 September to 5 November 2004 for a two-to-three week Snaresbrook trial fixed for 1 November.
Extensive enquiries had been made at Snaresbrook but not at other London Crown Court centres.
Judge Bing regarded a duty to enquire elsewhere as novel and found good cause in courtroom unavailability at Snaresbrook.
Mr Potter relied on ex parte MacDonald, Blair and the recent Bannister decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review application for permission and substantive relief against a Crown Court custody time limit extension.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; extension quashed and matter remitted to the Crown Court for reconsideration at the next mention on 31 August 2004.
enrichment.ratio: Where custody time limits are extended on grounds of judge or courtroom unavailability, the court must rigorously examine the cause and, on the authorities, positive steps should include enquiries at courts other than the designated trial centre before accepting listing difficulty as good and sufficient cause.
legal_issues: Whether listing office enquiries at other London courts were required
Application of ex parte MacDonald and Bannister to Crown Court extensions
Whether unavailability of a courtroom could justify a lengthy extension in a non-complex case
linked_authorities: R v Manchester Crown Court ex parte MacDonald [1999] 1 Cr App R 409
R (Bannister) v Crown Court at Guildford [2004] EWHC 221 (Admin)
R v Blair, Bryant and Taylor

notes: Category A and Wakefield transfer challenge dismissed; Golds assurance dispute unresolved without cross-examination.

enrichment.short_title: MJ v SSHD: Category A status and dispersal prison challenge dismissed
key_facts: A life-sentenced Category A rapist challenged maintenance of Category A status and transfer to HMP Wakefield to complete the Core Sex Offender Treatment Programme.
He claimed Mr Golds had promised he would never be placed in a dispersal prison if he gave evidence against another prisoner.
Prison reports recommended downgrading to Category B but the Category A Committee and DDG maintained Category A.
He argued Article 2 was engaged and that Pate required exceptional treatment outside dispersal prisons.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Category A categorisation decisions and allocation to HMP Wakefield.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; no oral hearing required; alleged Golds assurance not established without cross-examination.
enrichment.ratio: Prison categorisation decisions are subject to procedural fairness and full report disclosure but courts defer to Prison Service risk assessment; Article 2 is not engaged without a real and immediate risk to life; alleged promises about permanent non-dispersion must be proved and were not on the evidence accepted.
legal_issues: Whether an oral hearing was required for Category A review
Whether Mr Golds gave a legitimate expectation of permanent non-dispersion
Whether transfer to Wakefield engaged Article 2 ECHR
Whether prison reports made downgrading irrational and whether Pate was improperly fettered
linked_authorities: R (Pate) v Home Secretary [2002] EWHC 1018 (Admin)
R (Bloggs 61) v Home Secretary [2003] EWCA Civ 686
Osman v United Kingdom (1998) 29 EHRR 245

notes: Race discrimination appeal after EAT remittal; Tribunal reasons and inference analysis upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Madden v PTG: race discrimination and victimisation appeal dismissed
key_facts: Irish development technician George Madden was summarily dismissed after a grievance against his manager Mr Guest following an earlier unsuccessful direct race discrimination claim.
The employment tribunal found unfair and wrongful dismissal but dismissed direct discrimination and victimisation claims; the EAT remitted for inadequate reasons.
On remittal the tribunal analysed fourteen incidents, finding less favourable treatment in several but no racial or victimisation causation.
Keene LJ granted limited permission on motivation, inference, comparator and victimisation reasoning points.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of appeal against remitted employment tribunal liability decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; tribunal adequately explained refusal to draw inferences; less favourable treatment attributed to poor working relationship with Mr Guest, not Irish nationality or protected act.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal need not draw an inference of race discrimination merely because less favourable treatment and an inadequate explanation are found; hypothetical comparators need not be clones differing only in race; motive is irrelevant to the statutory tort but relevant evidentially; victimisation requires causation by the protected act.
legal_issues: Whether the tribunal misdirected itself that motive was irrelevant to inference drawing
Whether less favourable treatment plus no explanation obliged a race inference
Construction of hypothetical comparators under section 3(4)
Whether victimisation inferences were adequately explained
linked_authorities: King v Great Britain-China Centre [1991] IRLR 513
Shamoon v Chief Constable of the RUC [2003] IRLR 285
Nagarajan v London Regional Transport [1999] 1 AC 501

notes: Cinema covenant construction; cinema use within clause 12.2.2(a) but access not ancillary.

enrichment.short_title: GLN v Tunbridge Wells: cinema covenant and ancillary access use
key_facts: Former Essoldo cinema land was subject to ABC/Odeon covenants prohibiting cinema use and associated image-projection uses.
Tunbridge Wells Borough Council proposed a multi-screen cinema on adjoining land with pedestrian access over the burdened property via stairs, lift and concourse.
GLN collaborated with the council to obtain a declaration that such access would breach the covenant.
The deputy judge held cinema use was not within clause 12.2.2(a) but access would be ancillary under 12.2.2(b).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from declaratory judgment on construction of restrictive covenants in a 2000 transfer.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed in effect; cinema use falls within clause 12.2.2(a) but use of common parts for access to mixed retail/cinema development is not ancillary to a prohibited cinema use.
enrichment.ratio: Use as a cinema naturally falls within words prohibiting principal use for image projection of whole films despite partial overlap with an express cinema prohibition; ancillary use under a related clause looks to the principal purpose of the totality of premises served, so access shared substantially with large retail units is not ancillary to cinema use alone.
legal_issues: Whether cinema use is within clause 12.2.2(a) or only clause 12.2.1
Whether pedestrian access over burdened land to an off-site cinema is ancillary use
Whether the appeal was academic after covenantees withdrew
Redundancy in covenant drafting and restrained construction
linked_authorities: Co-operative Retail Services Ltd v Tesco Stores Ltd (1998) 76 P&CR 328
Elliot v Safeway Stores Plc [1999] 1 WLR 1396
Tea Trade Properties Ltd v CIN Properties Ltd [1990] 1 EGLR 150

confidence.notes: Construction issues clearly resolved though ancillary-use analysis is partly a question of degree.

notes: Patent revocation costs; two-week negotiation delay insufficient for indemnity costs.

enrichment.short_title: Affymetrix v Multilyte: indemnity costs refused after patent capitulation
key_facts: Affymetrix sought revocation and non-infringement declarations; Multilyte counterclaimed for infringement then ceased defending.
The court revoked two UK patents and dismissed the counterclaim.
Affymetrix sought standard costs overall but indemnity costs for 4–18 August when Multilyte stopped trial preparation and negotiated withdrawal.
Multilyte did not notify capitulation until 18 August though it had largely decided to withdraw on 4 August.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Costs application following consent order revoking patents and dismissing infringement counterclaim in patent proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Standard costs order only; indemnity costs refused for the two-week period because negotiation before withdrawal was not improper or unreasonable conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Indemnity costs require material impropriety or unreasonableness in conduct; taking two weeks to negotiate termination of proceedings before notifying withdrawal is reasonable and most costs in that period would be recoverable on the standard basis anyway.
legal_issues: Whether delay in notifying withdrawal justified indemnity costs
Whether continuing trial preparation while negotiating capitulation was unreasonable
Threshold for indemnity costs in interlocutory patent litigation

confidence.notes: Short costs judgment with clear ratio on indemnity threshold.

notes: Renewed permission refused; CDM regulations held inapplicable to public right of way claimant.

enrichment.short_title: Willis v Corn Exchange trustees: CDM regulations challenge refused
key_facts: Graham Willis tripped on a pipe on steps beside the Alnwick Corn Exchange over which there was a public right of way.
Volunteer trustees were demolishing inside the building and had hired a skip; the pipe had been placed in and removed from the skip by unknown persons.
The county court judge dismissed negligence claims, finding a skip in a residential street analogy insufficient to impose hirer liability for third-party acts.
Willis sought permission to appeal on breach of CDM and construction health and safety regulations.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal from county court dismissal of personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; regulations held primarily for protection of persons at work on the construction site, not members of the public on a nearby right of way.
enrichment.ratio: The 1996 construction health and safety regulations apply to construction work carried out by a person at work and their references to safe places of work concern workers on site, not pedestrians exercising a public right of way; the 1994 CDM regulations exclude civil liability except for regulation 16(1)(c), and the defendants were not the principal contractor.
legal_issues: Whether CDM and construction welfare regulations applied to a public right of way user
Whether a skip hirer owed duty for pipe discarded by unknown persons
Whether the judge erred in dismissing statutory duty claims

confidence.notes: Short permission judgment with clear statutory construction reasoning.

notes: GMC interim suspension extended six months pending performance assessment; costs summarily assessed.

enrichment.short_title: GMC v George: six-month extension of interim suspension pending assessment
key_facts: Dr Abraham George, a paediatrician, had been suspended since March 2003 pending fitness-to-practise proceedings.
The Interim Orders Committee on 9 June 2004 found cogent prima facie evidence of substandard practice, dysfunctional behaviour and lack of insight.
The GMC applied under section 41A(6) for a further 12-month suspension extension.
Performance assessment dates were fixed between September and November 2004 after earlier adjournments requested by the doctor.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by the GMC to extend an interim suspension order under section 41A(6) of the Medical Act 1983.
enrichment.outcome: Extension granted for six months until 5 March 2005 rather than twelve; defendant ordered to pay GMC costs summarily assessed at £3,000.
enrichment.ratio: The court has discretion to extend interim suspension where necessary to protect the public pending assessment; it would be irresponsible to allow a doctor to resume practice before completion of a lawfully ordered performance assessment, but the extension should match the time needed for assessment and review rather than automatically granting the full period sought.
legal_issues: Whether extension of interim suspension was necessary and proportionate
Whether suspension pending assessment placed the doctor at evidential disadvantage
Appropriate length of extension where assessment was imminent
Costs where the doctor contested any extension

notes: No concluded ACE contract; arbitration clause not engaged despite fee negotiations and signed memorandum.

enrichment.short_title: Gurney v Pearson: no arbitration agreement without executed ACE contract
key_facts: Consulting engineers Gurney provided structural engineering services on a Beauchamp Place refurbishment for pension fund trustees.
Negotiations contemplated an ACE Agreement 3 with BPF collateral warranty but no jointly executed formal appointment was completed.
Part of the front wall collapsed on 26 October 1998; the trustees later sought arbitration under ACE clause 4.
Gurney contended it worked pending contract only and that telephone and letter negotiations never concluded all terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial of whether a contract incorporating ACE standard terms and an arbitration clause had been concluded.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that there was no valid arbitration agreement; no contract concluded between trustees and Gurney.
enrichment.ratio: Parties intended to be bound only by formal execution of an ACE memorandum with completed client details and BPF warranty terms; negotiations remained invitations to treat and incomplete on essential documentary terms despite fee agreement, invoices and a unilateral signed memorandum never accepted by the client.
legal_issues: Whether contract was concluded by correspondence or telephone negotiation in May 1998
Whether parties intended binding interim agreement pending formal ACE execution
Whether Mr Rose's signed memorandum sent in November 1998 constituted acceptance
Application of Pagnan and Trentham principles to partly performed professional services

G Percy Trentham Ltd v Archital Luxfer Ltd [1993] 1 Lloyd's Rep 25

notes: Category D recategorisation quashed where conduct since open allocation not evidenced as considered.

enrichment.short_title: Vary and Riordan: category D downgrade quashed for failure to consider conduct
key_facts: Following escape of prisoner MacLean, the Prison Service reviewed 22 category D prisoners with more than five years to non-parole release.
Michael Riordan and John Caetano, serving 20-year drug sentences, were abruptly moved from open conditions to closed prisons and recategorised C with identical RC1 reasons.
Riordan had unescorted transfer, enhanced status, no adjudications and a successful town visit before the review.
The revised policy emphasised sentence length, offence seriousness and public confidence in open placement of long-term prisoners.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited judicial review of recategorisation from category D to category C following MacLean escape policy review.
enrichment.outcome: Recategorisation decisions set aside; defendant directed to reconsider grading with an open mind on all material available at the date of the fresh decision; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A lawful policy change may be applied to prisoners already in category D, but individual review must take into account conduct and circumstances since allocation, including successful open-prison progress; identical boilerplate reasons and failure to show conduct was considered render the decision procedurally unfair and Wednesbury unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether revised category D policy could lawfully be applied retrospectively
Whether claimants had a legitimate expectation of retaining category D status
Whether individual conduct since open allocation was considered
Whether boilerplate RC1 reasons demonstrated proper individual review
linked_authorities: Re Findlay [1985] 1 AC 318
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Hargreaves [1997] 1 WLR 407
R (North and East Devon Health Authority) ex parte Coughlan [2001] QB 213

notes: Service charge leave-to-appeal JR; Sivasubramaniam discretion and Lane v Esdaile analysis are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Sinclair Gardens: judicial review of Lands Tribunal refusal of leave from LVT
key_facts: The landlord of 75 Eardley Crescent challenged an LVT decision disallowing various service charge items including damp proofing works.
The LVT and then the Lands Tribunal refused leave to appeal against the June 2003 LVT decision.
The landlord sought judicial review, contending there was no appeal to the Court of Appeal and that the refusal was Wednesbury unreasonable.
The tenants were largely unrepresented while the landlord was legally represented on wider jurisdictional issues.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Lands Tribunal's refusal of permission to appeal from a Leasehold Valuation Tribunal service charge decision.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; refusal of permission to appeal by the Lands Tribunal is not a section 3(4) decision appealable to the Court of Appeal, and Sivasubramaniam limits judicial review to exceptional circumstances not present here.
enrichment.ratio: A refusal of permission to appeal by the Lands Tribunal under section 31A(6) is not a 'decision' for section 3(4) of the Lands Tribunal Act 1949, following Lane v Esdaile; judicial review of such refusals should ordinarily be refused unless exceptional jurisdictional or procedural circumstances exist, as in Sivasubramaniam.
legal_issues: Whether a Lands Tribunal refusal of leave to appeal from an LVT is a section 3(4) decision
Whether judicial review should be available to bypass the service charge statutory scheme
Whether Sivasubramaniam applies to tribunal refusals of permission to appeal
Whether the refusal was Wednesbury unreasonable or involved jurisdictional error
linked_authorities: R (Sivasubramaniam) v Wandsworth County Court [2003] 1 WLR 475
Lane v Esdaile [1891] AC 210
Bland v Chief Supplementary Benefit Officer [1983] 1 WLR 262

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme, Lane v Esdaile reasoning and final dismissal are all clearly reasoned.
